item.text: {"verdicts":[{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0027-R02-E001","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0027-R02-E002","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0027-R02-E003","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"Formal employment was higher among men, urban residents, and northern states than in southern Mexico; Nuevo León, Coahuila, and Chihuahua had the highest rates, while Chiapas and Oaxaca had the lowest. Almost all formal employment in the southern region was in the public sector, while about 95% of the country's work was generated by the private sector. The proportion of women outside the labor market but available for work was more than double that of men.","notes":["The excerpt states that the proportion of women in this category was more than double men's; it does not state a precise person-count ratio of more than two to one."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0027-R02-E004","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"Between 2005 and 2017, Mexico experienced wage compression toward the bottom: the share of men earning more than five minimum wages declined, women were disproportionately concentrated at very low wages, and low-paid work was concentrated in rural areas and was mostly informal. Real labor income declined across occupations, genders, and age groups; bottom-40% hourly median wages were stagnant while the top-60% median contracted by about 15%.","notes":["The excerpt specifically reports a reduction in the share of men earning more than five minimum wages, not a general decline in all high-wage employment."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0027-R02-E005","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0027-R02-E006","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0027-R02-E007","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0027-R02-E008","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]}]}
